FoveaNav learns task-relevant gaze for robust visual navigation.
The Fovea policy selects where to look.
The selected gaze becomes a Gaussian gaze map.
The navigation transformer uses this map to predict a future trajectory from the full image.
The navigation transformer is trained with BC, while the Fovea policy is trained with RL using a reward based on trajectory prediction error.

We evaluate FoveaNav with closed-loop real-robot deployment across five navigation tasks.
The first task is red bag following.
The robot follows a person carrying a red bag.
We compare our method with a full-image behavior cloning baseline.
In the in-distribution setting, both methods predict similar trajectories.
However, FoveaNav shifts its gaze to track the task-relevant target.
The attention and occlusion sensitivity maps also show more concentrated responses around the red bag.
In the OOD setting, we add red distractors that can be confused with the target.
Our method checks nearby obstacles, then refocuses on the red bag to keep following the target.
In the OOD setting, BC achieves a success rate of twenty percent, compared with ninety percent for ours.
The BC baseline fails to identify the red bag among distractors and ends in a collision.
BC also fails under other visual changes outside the training distribution, such as background changes, while ours remains robust.

In obstacle avoidance, the robot must avoid obstacles while staying on the track.
In the in-distribution setting, where obstacle types match those in the training data, both FoveaNav and BC successfully complete the track.
The OOD setting introduces unseen obstacle types and changes in obstacle placement.
Here, the two models again differ in performance.
Our method directs its gaze toward obstacle boundaries and free space.
With this gaze, the attention and occlusion sensitivity maps show concentrated responses around the obstacles.
BC often fails to avoid unseen obstacles.
In the OOD setting, ours achieves a success rate of ninety percent, compared with zero percent for BC.

In sign-guided navigation, the robot follows arrow signs at junctions and stops at the goal sign.
FoveaNav moves its gaze toward the arrow when making a turn.
With changed sign locations and background appearance, BC often predicts the wrong direction.
Our method focuses on the arrow cue and makes the correct turn.
In the OOD setting for this task, ours achieves a success rate of ninety-six percent, compared with thirty-eight percent for BC.

In screen-cue navigation, the robot uses a screen instruction to choose the target box.
FoveaNav moves its gaze between the screen and the boxes, using task-dependent visual cues.
We evaluate this task under in-distribution conditions. The success rates are about eighty percent for ours and thirty percent for BC.

In forest following, the robot follows a person outdoors.
When a distractor appears, FoveaNav stays focused on the target, while BC turns toward the distractor.
Under OOD conditions, BC fails every trial, while ours succeeds every time.
Across five navigation tasks, FoveaNav maintains in-distribution performance and improves robustness to OOD visual changes.
Learning where to look provides a useful inductive bias for robust visual navigation.
